payload.text: I read this as deep research on memory representation and prompt rendering - I’ll gather primary-source schemas, empirical format/context evidence, rewrite and auditability precedents, then synthesize a cited evidence table and recommendation without code changes.

I’ve completed the shipped-system/schema pass and am now triangulating it against primary papers and public implementation sources. The clearest early pattern is that storage and injection are separate design choices: production systems often keep granular, provenance-bearing records even when they expose or inject a compact prose view.

I read this as evidence synthesis on memory representation and prompt rendering - I’ll separate documented facts from inference, expose evidence gaps, and recommend a storage/rendering design.

## Bottom line

**Recommendation: use a hybrid architecture.**

1. **Canonical store:** atomic, independently addressable memory records with timestamps, status, confidence, and source provenance.
2. **Retrieval:** select a small task-relevant subset rather than injecting the entire memory.
3. **Prompt rendering:** render retrieved records into a concise, labeled natural-language list inside a clearly delimited section, optionally XML-wrapped.
4. **Narrative summaries:** maintain them only as derived caches or retrieval keys, never as the sole source of truth.
5. **Updates:** append or target individual records; do not regenerate the whole memory for routine edits.

That is the strongest combination of:
- production-system precedent,
- auditability,
- resistance to rewrite clobbering,
- temporal updates,
- and current evidence that larger/more complex prompts reduce reliable adherence.

---

## Evidence table

**Strength scale**

- **High:** primary schema/source code, official API documentation, or controlled empirical paper.
- **Medium:** official product behavior without public backend schema, or a benchmark related but not identical to persistent user memory.
- **Low:** vendor guidance without published evaluation, or architectural inference.

---

## Comparative judgment

| Representation | Storage quality | Prompt usability | Update safety | Auditability | Judgment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic fact records only | Strong | Can become noisy if dumped raw | Strong | Strong | Best canonical representation, poor if indiscriminately injected |
| One generated narrative summary | Compact and coherent | Strong for broad personalization | Weak under repeated whole rewrites | Weak unless separately linked to sources | Useful cache/view, unsafe sole source of truth |
| Labeled free-text blocks | Good for stable domains and human editing | Strong | Moderate with targeted edits; weak with full rewrites | Moderate | Good prompt-facing layer, not sufficient canonical store |
| Hybrid atomic store + derived/rendered text | Strong | Strong | Strong | Strong | **Recommended** |

---

## Recommended design

### 1. Canonical record

Store one independently addressable proposition, preference, instruction, decision, or event per record:

```text
id
subject / scope
kind: preference | constraint | fact | event | decision
text
status: active | superseded | disputed | expired
valid_from / valid_to
created_at / updated_at
confidence
source_episode_ids[]
supersedes_id?
sensitivity / visibility
```

This follows the useful portions of Mem0’s atomic records and Graphiti’s temporal/provenance-bearing edges rather than copying either schema literally: https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/blob/4debc58a83377b18be81ae1e5969a300736b2fac/mem0/configs/base.py and https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/blob/401c59a65bdeb22a44136901ff30231e6998a7fe/graphiti_core/edges.py.

Do not erase contradicted consequential records; mark them superseded or invalidated so the decision trail survives, as Graphiti’s valid/invalid times and W3C PROV revisions permit: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956 and https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/.

### 2. Retrieval budget

Retrieve by task relevance, active status, scope, recency where applicable, and decision importance.

A reasonable starting policy is:

- **3–5 active behavioral constraints/preferences**
- **5–10 supporting facts/events**
- normally **under roughly 500–1,000 prompt tokens**
- expand only for explicit memory-recall or audit requests

The exact numbers are a design prior, not a proven universal threshold. FollowBench’s GPT-4 result—84.7% hard adherence with one constraint versus 61.9% with five—justifies keeping the active constraint set small: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.20410. Lost-in-the-Middle and RULER justify avoiding “inject everything because the model supports 128K”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654.

### 3. Prompt rendering

Render natural-language memory text, not raw database JSON:

```xml
<relevant_memory>
Use these only when relevant to the current request.
Current explicit instructions override conflicting memories.

<preferences>
- [m_104] User prefers concise answers.
- [m_219] User wants temperatures in Celsius.
</preferences>

<relevant_facts>
- [m_331] User is preparing a presentation for the finance team.
</relevant_facts>
</relevant_memory>
```

Why this form:

- concise prose matches real Mem0 and Graphiti integrations: https://docs.mem0.ai/integrations/chatdev and https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/blob/401c59a65bdeb22a44136901ff30231e6998a7fe/examples/langgraph-agent/agent.ipynb;
- labels separate behavioral constraints from merely descriptive facts;
- IDs preserve a route back to provenance without spending tokens on full metadata;
- XML is a delimiter, not the underlying data model; Anthropic recommends such separation, but the choice should still be tested per target model: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/use-xml-tags and https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11324.

Place high-priority behavioral memories near the controlling system instructions rather than buried in retrieved documents. Put the current user request after long supporting context when the model family benefits from query-at-end placement; Anthropic reports up to a 30% improvement in its tests for complex multi-document inputs: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/use-xml-tags.

### 4. Narrative summaries

Generate summaries at user/project/topic scope only as:

- a human-readable overview,
- a retrieval key,
- or a compact fallback when individual records exceed budget.

The summary should contain referenced record IDs or retain a machine-side membership list. Rebuild it from active canonical records, never use it to overwrite them. LongMemEval supports summaries and extracted facts as retrieval keys while warning that compressed representations can lose information if they replace retained values: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10813.

### 5. Update protocol

Use:

- append for new information;
- targeted record update or supersession for corrections;
- exact-match/diff operations for free-text block maintenance;
- occasional full compaction only from canonical records, with before/after coverage checks.

Letta explicitly prohibits whole-block replacement for small changes, and both Letta and Anthropic reject ambiguous exact replacements: https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L311-L376 and https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool.

A compactor should verify that every active consequential record is either represented in the new summary or deliberately excluded with a reason. This mitigation is **INFERRED engineering practice**; no located paper supplies a reliable per-rewrite omission rate.

### 6. Audit path

For any consequential output, log:

- retrieved memory IDs and versions,
- their source episode IDs,
- the rendered memory block,
- the model/prompt version,
- and which memory records were cited or materially used.

This is compatible with Graphiti’s source-episode links and W3C PROV’s source, derivation, revision, attribution, and invalidation model: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956 and https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/.

---

## Strongest counterargument

The strongest case for a **single editable narrative summary** is operational simplicity: the model sees one coherent portrait instead of fragmented facts; users can inspect and edit it; cross-fact implications are pre-integrated; and Claude shipped exactly this project-scoped design in 2025: https://www.anthropic.com/news/memory.

That argument is fair. Atomic retrieval can omit a relevant record, over-rank stale fragments, or present internally inconsistent bullets. Narrative organization may improve broad personalization where no single query retrieves all useful background.

It is still not enough to make the summary canonical. Claude’s newer documented flow stores individual entries, LongMemEval finds value in decomposition and retained source values, Zep substantially outperforms recursive summarization on DMR, and targeted-edit tooling exists precisely to avoid unnecessary whole-state rewrites: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12123587-import-and-export-your-memory-from-claude, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10813, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956, and https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool.

**Final judgment:** preserve atomic truth and provenance; retrieve narrowly; render compact labeled prose; treat narrative summaries as disposable projections.
